meta.title: ModelHub — We measure models. Not marketing.
meta.description: Open ranking of frontier AI models. Third-party numbers, no marketing, with the source and the date in plain sight.

masthead.blurb: Closed and open-weights models on the same field. Numbers come from third-party evaluations and human voting; what the vendor claims never counts toward the score.

panel.degradedSource: {source} has not responded since {since}; showing its {snapshot} snapshot
panel.ruleSkipped: Releases it published that were passed over: {list}.
panel.agingSource: {source} has not published new numbers in {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} (last: {date})

filters.label: Filters
filters.showing: {count, plural, one {# model} other {# models}} of {total}
filters.unknownHidden: Models with no listed price or context are hidden while these filters are on.

table.agedCategoryTitle: The newest release that carries this category is from {date}, {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} ago
table.provisionalNote: These models have fewer than {min} of {total} categories measured. They stay visible but don't compete for a slot: spreading the weight across only the available categories lifts a thinly measured model on what it is missing, not on being better.
table.awaitingVotesTitle: Has the benchmarks but hasn't accumulated LMArena votes yet. This is not a penalty.
table.errorUnknownTitle: None of this model's sources publish their error. The interval is unknown, not zero.
table.rankDesc: Significance rank: a model sits at one plus the number of models measurably ahead of it. A number prefixed with = is a joint placing, meaning the 95% intervals overlap and the measurement does not separate those models.
table.compositeDesc: Weighted composite out of 100, followed by the half-width of a 95% interval. That interval is a floor, not an estimate: inputs that publish no error contribute zero, so the real interval can only be wider. ±? means no source published an error at all, which is unknown rather than zero.
table.coverageDesc: Five segments, one per category, filled where that category was measured. Beside it, the number of benchmarks standing behind the composite — a different question from how many categories were covered.
table.priceTitle: Blended price in USD per million tokens, at the input:output ratio set in config/weights.json
table.frontierTitle: Cost frontier: no other priced model costs the same or less and scores the same or more
table.legendFrontier: on the cost frontier (see the chart above)
table.legendNone: not measured; hover for the reason when it is known

footer.methodNote: The composite weights Reasoning 25 · Coding 25 · Math 20 · Human preference 15 · Instructions 15. Multimodal is measured separately and stays out of the composite: penalising a text-only model for a category it does not compete in would invent a difference that isn't there.
footer.sourceNote: Sources: Epoch AI (CC-BY-4.0), LMArena (CC-BY-4.0) and LiveBench (Apache-2.0). Every run lands as an auditable commit in the repo.
footer.swebenchNote: SWE-bench Verified comes from Epoch's own runs. The agentic scaffold leaderboard at swebench.com is not ingested because its CC-BY-NC licence conflicts with this MIT repo:

compare.title: Compare models
compare.intro: Pick two to four models. The bars share a 0–100 axis, so lengths are directly comparable across categories and across models.
compare.selected: {count, plural, one {# of {max} selected} other {# of {max} selected}}
compare.empty: Select at least one model to compare.
compare.tableView: The same numbers, as a table
compare.visionNote: Outside the composite. Measured separately, because a text-only model doesn't compete here.
compare.full: Maximum reached — remove a model first
compare.notSeparatedTitle: The gap between these two composites ({gap}) is smaller than their combined 95% interval (±{combined}). The measurement does not separate them, so no difference is claimed.
compare.deltaNote: Δ is measured against the first selected model. Where the gap falls inside the two models' combined interval it reads "not separated": the same rule the ranking uses, applied here so a difference smaller than the error never looks like a win.

local.title: What runs on my machine?
local.metaTitle: What runs on my machine? — ModelHub
local.metaDescription: Enter your GPU, memory and RAM and see which measured open-weights models fit, at what quantisation and at about what speed. Estimates from model size, ordered by composite.
local.intro: Enter your hardware and see which measured open-weights models fit in its memory, and at about what speed. These are estimates from model size, not measurements on your machine. The list is ordered by composite, never by how comfortably a model fits.

hardware.title: Your hardware
hardware.presetNote: Presets only fill in numbers. They are listed alphabetically and none is a recommendation. Laptop GPUs are not listed because their memory bus varies; use custom values.
hardware.ramHint: Installed RAM. About 10% is held back for the system.
hardware.bandwidthHint: Optional. Without it, GPU speed is not estimated.
hardware.invalid: Enter the memory figures above to see what fits.

hints.noGpu: This browser does not expose WebGPU.
hints.memory: Memory reported by the browser: at least {gb} GB (browsers cap this figure at 8).
hints.noMemory: This browser does not report memory.

import.body: Run llmfit recommend --json in a terminal and paste what it prints. It is read inside this page and never uploaded.

import.applied: Hardware filled in from the import.
import.error_too_large: That is too large to be a recommend list.

results.fitsEmpty: No ranked model fits this hardware at this context.
results.provisionalNote: Measured in fewer than 4 of 5 categories, so they hold no rank. Listed alphabetically.
results.doesNotCount: {count, plural, one {# model does not fit} other {# models do not fit}}

row.halved: Context cut to {tokens} tokens to fit.

notes.title: How to read this
notes.estimates: Every figure is an estimate from parameter count, quantisation, context and memory bandwidth. Real speed depends on the runtime, the driver and what else is using memory.
notes.moe: Mixture-of-experts models are sized on active parameters for speed. On a GPU that holds all the experts, that is an upper bound.
notes.layout: {withLayout, plural, one {# of {total} models has} other {# of {total} models have}} a recorded hybrid-attention layout. The others are sized as full attention, which over-states their memory.
notes.unsized: {count, plural, one {# open-weights model has} other {# open-weights models have}} no size on record and is not listed here.
notes.order: Order is by composite (ties shown as =k), then name. Fit never reorders the list.
notes.method: Method, constants and attribution: see the methodology.

model.descriptionPending: Description pending. Editorial descriptions are generated by Layer B using a local model and approved by a person before publishing; it hasn't been run for this model yet.
model.partialNote: Partial composite: no measurement for {missing}. The weight is spread across the available categories only, and the model is flagged rather than zero-filled.
model.historyRange: {points, plural, one {# observation} other {# observations}}, {from} to {to}
model.historyScope: The history available today comes from LMArena, the only source that publishes its full time series. Epoch and LiveBench publish point-in-time snapshots, so their history accumulates run by run from the day the daily ingest started.
model.historyBreaks: The window starts on 2026-01-01, after Arena's most recent methodology change. That is why this line can be drawn continuous without lying: it doesn't cross a break.
model.acquisitionPending: Pending. Acquisition links (HuggingFace repo, provider page, API docs, Ollama tag) are assembled deterministically by Layer B; the fields exist in the schema and stay empty until then.
model.acquisitionWithheld: {count, plural, one {# unverified, withheld pending manual review} other {# unverified, withheld pending manual review}}
model.configurationNote: Every number below describes the {variant} variant as the vendor published it. One configuration is chosen for the whole model: taking each benchmark's best would describe a setup nobody runs.
model.configurationPlain: Every number below describes the variant the vendor published without an effort qualifier.
model.configurationMismatch: Human preference is the exception: LMArena never published the {variant} variant, so that vote measures {measured}. The figure is kept and the difference stated, rather than discarding real human votes over a naming difference between sources.
model.uncertaintyNote: The ±{error} is the half-width of a 95% interval on the composite, and it is a floor rather than an estimate: {measured} of {total} inputs publish their error and the rest contribute zero. The real interval can only be wider, never narrower.
model.uncertaintyNone: None of this model's sources publish a margin of error, so its composite carries no interval. That means "unknown", not "exact": its place in the table is the least defensible of any, because it is compared as a point value.
model.uncertaintyTied: It shares a rank with {count, plural, one {# other model} other {# other models}} because their intervals overlap.
model.recalibration: Cohort recalibration, not a change in measurement. Its normalised human preference value moved {normalized} points while its Arena rating changed only {raw}: a model with an extreme rating joined or left and the scale shifted underneath. The effect on the composite is {composite} points — above {threshold}, this run's median gap between neighbours — and nobody voted differently to cause it.
model.metaDescription: Composite, coverage and sources of {name} ({provider}), from third-party evaluations and human voting, each with its date.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: Everything here can be reproduced by hand from the public JSON in the repository. If a number on this site disagrees with this page, the site is wrong.

formula.title: The composite, exactly
formula.body: Each benchmark is placed on a 0–100 scale. Within a category the available benchmarks are averaged, and those categories are weighted like this:
formula.inputs_coding: SWE-bench Verified (Epoch) · LiveBench Coding and Agentic Coding
formula.singleSourceNote: "Single source" marks categories that depend on one data provider: if that source goes down, the whole category gets no new snapshot, not just one benchmark inside it.
formula.equation: composite = Σ(category score × weight) ÷ Σ(weight of categories with data)
formula.normalisation: Benchmarks already reported as percentages are used as-is. LMArena's Bradley-Terry ratings are not percentages, so they are min-max normalised against the cohort present in each build: in the current build, {min} and {max} are the 0 and the 100. This means a model's normalised Arena value can move even when its rating doesn't, if a model enters or leaves either extreme.
formula.multimodal: Multimodal stays out of the composite and is shown as a separate vision score. Including a category most text models don't compete in would mean penalising them for an absence that says nothing about their quality.
formula.knowledge: SimpleQA Verified (Epoch) measures factual knowledge, not reasoning. It feeds the Knowledge board and takes no part in the composite, so no knowledge benchmark moves a model's Reasoning score.

releases.title: {source}: which release each category comes from
releases.body: {source} publishes dated releases, and a newer one does not always publish every suite an older one did, nor measure on the same scale. Each category is therefore decided on its own, from a measurement. We take the newest release that publishes the category's suite and compare it with the nearest earlier release that publishes a different suite, using the mean absolute gap between the two on the models both measured.
releases.comparable: If that gap is at most {maxDrift} points, and at least {minCommon} models are shared, the two scales count as one: the newest release is used, and a model it lacks keeps its value from the older release, dated with that release.
releases.notComparable: If the gap is larger, or too few models are shared to tell, the category comes from a single release: the one covering more models, the newest on a tie. Two scales are never mixed inside one category.
releases.single: A category with no earlier release to compare against uses the newest release as published. The thresholds live in config/sources.json and are debatable by PR.

reason.comparable: comparable: newest release, older values fill gaps
reason.not_comparable_more_coverage_older: not comparable: the older release covers more models
reason.not_comparable_more_coverage_newest: not comparable: the newest release covers more models
reason.too_few_common_models: too few shared models to compare: newest release only

releases.limits: Limits: the gap is a mean over the models both releases measured, so it says nothing about models only one of them measured, and with few shared models it is a weak estimate, which is why a minimum is required. A category taken from an older release is as old as that release, and its column header says so.

coverage.title: The coverage gate
coverage.body: A model needs data in at least 4 of the 5 categories to enter the main ranking. Below that it appears in the Provisional section: visible, with its composite computed, but without a rank number.
coverage.example: This exists because of a real problem. Since the weight is spread across only the categories that have data, a thinly measured model rises on what it is MISSING rather than on being better. Qwen3-Max-Instruct, with 3 of 5 categories, was landing at rank 5, above models measured on all five. That is precisely the bias this site exists to fight, so it is corrected in code rather than in a footnote.
coverage.newModels: The threshold is 4 and not 5 on purpose. A newly released model can have all four benchmarks and no LMArena votes yet; that case ranks normally, flagged as awaiting human votes. Sufficient evidence is required; being new is not punished.
coverage.current: In the current build: {ranked} ranked models and {provisional} provisional, with the threshold at {min} of 5.
coverage.scope: The whole catalogue also has a cutoff date: only models published on or after {date} are eligible at all. That is not a measurement threshold like the one above - it is a scope filter, and it decides which models exist on the site before anything is measured. The value lives in config/weights.json, with its reasoning documented right there, and is debatable by PR like any other number on this page.

variants.title: Variants of the same model
variants.body: A vendor publishes the same model under several configurations: effort levels, thinking modes. They are the same weights with a different inference budget, so they are grouped under one canonical model. That forces a decision about which value to use when a benchmark arrives more than once, and the decision moves the ranking.
variants.bug: The concrete case: Claude Opus 5 had three variants in LiveBench, and all three entered the Coding category average separately. That benchmark outweighed Epoch 3 to 1, not because it measured better, but because the vendor published more variants. Fixing it changed the top three: GPT-5.6 Sol fell to #3 and Muse Spark 1.1 rose to #2.
variants.tradeoff: We choose a single configuration per model and use it across all of its benchmarks; when a benchmark did not measure that configuration, we leave the gap — and the coverage drops — rather than substituting a different configuration.
variants.principle: This is the same principle applied to SWE-bench scaffolds: reveal the configuration, don't hide it. The mechanisms differ — a scaffold is another system, by another author, contributing much of the result; an effort level is the same weights with a different knob — but the principle is identical, and in both cases it exists for the same reason: to stop a published number from describing a configuration nobody ran.
variants.disclosure: That is why the configuration is never hidden: on each model page, the sources table states exactly which variant produced each number and how many were published.
variants.option_model: choose ONE configuration for the whole model and use it across every benchmark: the effort label with the widest coverage wins, ties going to the variant published without a qualifier. If a benchmark never measured that configuration, the cell is left empty and coverage reflects it. This is the current value.
variants.option_default: use, benchmark by benchmark, the variant published without an effort qualifier; if none exists, fall back to the best. Rejected as the default because it chooses separately per benchmark: a model could take max-effort in Math and xhigh in Coding, a configuration nobody runs.
variants.option_best: use the highest score across variants. It reflects the model's ceiling, but rewards publishing more variants: the maximum of five draws beats the maximum of one.
variants.option_average: average the variants. Rejected as the default: nobody runs 'the mean effort level', so it invents a configuration that does not exist, understating the peak and overstating the cheap variant.
variants.option_separate: do not group; treat each variant as its own model. This is the most consistent with the scaffold rule, but it is not viable today: each source names variants differently (Epoch uses '_max', LiveBench '-max-effort', LMArena '-high'), so without grouping we would hand-maintain an alias table per variant per source. That collides with the zero-daily-maintenance constraint, and it would fragment coverage enough to empty the main ranking. Not implemented.
variants.current: Every affected number states on the model page which configuration was used. Under the current policy the unqualified variant wins most often, followed by xhigh, high and max. When a benchmark never measured the chosen configuration we prefer to leave the gap and lower the coverage rather than substitute another one: a composite with one cell fewer is more honest than one that mixes configurations.
variants.arena: Human preference takes part in choosing the configuration, but only as a tie-breaker: when two labels cover the same benchmarks, the one LMArena also measured wins, because it is the only one that can be reported end to end. Giving it a full vote was tried on 2026-08-03 and rejected with the measurement in hand: a single Arena row overturned labels four benchmarks already agreed on, and against that day's cohort it cost Claude Opus 4.6 every LiveBench score and 17.88 composite points.
variants.mismatch: Where LMArena never published the chosen configuration, its row is kept here — the best-determined one, with the most votes — and the model page states which variant it measures. This is the deliberate exception to the leave-the-gap rule, and the reason is that the vocabularies are not comparable: Epoch labels effort levels ("_max", "_high") while Arena mostly publishes a plain name and a thinking variant. On a benchmark, a missing configuration means it was not measured; on Arena it usually means it is named differently. Dropping it was measured on 2026-08-03 and cost human preference on 21 of 43 models in that cohort: discarding real human votes over a naming difference trades a known measurement for none.
variants.mismatchBest: What did not survive in any case is picking the Arena row by highest rating. That is the "best" policy this project rejected in writing, applied silently to 15% of the weight: it flattered every model with a strong variant. Today, when a choice has to be made without a label match, the row with the most votes wins. Measured on 2026-08-03, the change took 11.6 rating points on average — 22.7 in the worst case — off the 6 models it affected then.

dedup.title: The LMArena duplication guard
dedup.body: LMArena snapshots are sometimes published with several rows per model, carrying different ratings and repeated ranks. Taking them at face value would break the ranking visibly.
dedup.example: A concrete case: the 2026-07-21 snapshot returns 1,113 rows for the overall category spread across only 378 distinct models, with rank 1 appearing three times at three different ratings. The 2026-07-20 snapshot has the same problem. The 2026-06-04 one is clean: 365 rows, 365 models.
dedup.rule: The rule: if rows ÷ distinct models exceeds 1.2, the whole snapshot is rejected and the ingest falls back to the last clean one. It is not 'repaired' by guessing which of the three rows is the real one. The same test is applied to the history, so trajectories don't inherit duplicated snapshots either. Rejections are recorded in data/status.json.

sourceTypes.title: Where a number is allowed to come from
sourceTypes.body: Every score records what kind of source it came from. The distinction is not decorative: it decides whether the number enters the composite.
sourceTypes.human_eval: blind human voting, such as LMArena. Enters the composite.
sourceTypes.third_party_benchmark: an evaluation run by an independent third party, such as Epoch AI or LiveBench. Enters the composite.
sourceTypes.vendor_claim: a figure published by whoever sells the model. Stored and displayed, but NEVER entered into the composite.
sourceTypes.why: A vendor has a direct incentive to pick the setup that flatters it, and there is no way to audit a run it never published. The exclusion is therefore structural rather than a case-by-case judgement: it doesn't depend on whether we happen to trust a given company.

contamination.title: Training contamination
contamination.body: A contaminated benchmark is one whose questions or answers show up in the data a model was trained on, inflating the score without measuring real capability. This site never attenuates a score for suspected contamination - doing so would be fabricating a number from an estimate. What it does instead is log public evidence, with its link, next to the affected score, in config/contamination.json.
contamination.empty: Reviewed on {date}. No benchmark has logged evidence yet. That is a checkable claim about what has been logged as of today, not a promise that no benchmark here has ever been contaminated.
contamination.count: Reviewed on {date}. {count, plural, one {# benchmark has} other {# benchmarks have}} public evidence on record, flagged on every affected model's page next to the source link.

derived.title: Derived metrics: cost and “best by”
derived.body: Three things on this site are computed from the composite and from a price, and none of them feeds back into the composite. A model's price cannot change its score, its rank or whether it clears the coverage gate. They are produced by the ingest, with no model involved, and are recomputable from data/models.json and data/best_by.json.
derived.blend: Price is blended into one figure per model: USD per million tokens at {input} input to {output} output, that is (input price × {input} + output price × {output}) ÷ {total}. The ratio is a convention, not a measurement of anyone's usage. It lives in config/weights.json and is debatable by PR. Prices come from the OpenRouter catalogue, dated per model, without long-prompt tiers.
derived.ratio: Price per composite point is the blended price divided by the composite. It is computed only for ranked models that have a price: {evaluated} in this build. The ratio says what each point costs on average. It does not say the points are the ones you need, and a low composite at a low price gives a low ratio, so read it next to the composite.
derived.pareto: The cost frontier marks a model when no other evaluated model costs the same or less and scores the same or more, with at least one strictly better. In this build, {members} of {evaluated} models are on it. The test compares point values and ignores intervals. Requiring the other model's interval to clear this one's was measured on 2026-11-05: 8 members instead of 7. The 3:1 blend was compared with 1:1 and 1:3 the same day, and the frontier did not change.
derived.unevaluated: A model with no price or without a rank is not evaluated, which is different from being dominated: its flag is empty, not false. Today {unpriced} ranked models have no price and are outside both the ratio and the frontier.
derived.rules: The “best by” cards come from the rules in config/weights.json under boards. Each rule names a metric and a filter, never a model or a provider. Only ranked models take part, so a provisional model never holds a first place. The rules in this build, with how many models each one can choose from:
derived.rule_under_1_usd: Composite, blended price at or below 1 USD per million tokens
derived.rule_cheapest_covered: Lowest blended price among models with at least 4 of 5 categories
derived.ties: A rule returns every model that no other candidate is measurably ahead of, using the same test as the rank: B is ahead of A when B's value minus its error exceeds A's value plus its error. When more than one model remains, they are reported as a tie, in the same way as the table. A metric without an interval, such as price, separates models only on exact equality.
derived.cheapest: The cheapest rule only says which model costs least among those with enough coverage. It says nothing about how well that model scores, and it is not a recommendation.

breaks.title: LMArena's methodology breaks
breaks.body: LMArena has changed how its rating is computed three times. Figures either side of a change are not comparable with each other:
breaks.window: Drawing a continuous line across a break would invent a trend that never happened. That is why the history window starts on 2026-01-01, after the most recent break: the plotted series doesn't cross one. Anyone moving that date earlier has to annotate the breaks or cut the series at the last one.

exclusions.title: What was left out, and why
exclusions.swebench: The swebench.com leaderboard is excluded on licensing grounds: its data is CC-BY-NC (non-commercial) and this repository is MIT, which does permit commercial use. Shipping that data here would hand anyone who forks the project a licence promising more rights than they actually have. The SWE-bench Verified figures that are used come from Epoch AI's own CC-BY licensed runs. Beyond the licence there is a technical reason: swebench.com rows describe agent scaffolds rather than bare models, and the scaffold often matters more than the model.
exclusions.others: Also excluded: HuggingFace's Open LLM Leaderboard, whose Space still reports as running while its results dataset hasn't moved since March 2025, and aider's Polyglot leaderboard, frozen since October 2025 even though the project itself is alive. Mixing 2025 figures with 2026 figures in a ranking whose whole premise is currency would be worse than omitting them.

reproduce.title: How to check it yourself
reproduce.body: There is no external database. Everything feeding this page is a versioned text file:
reproduce.git: Every daily run lands as a commit. That means any change to any number is an auditable diff: you can see when it changed, by how much, and which run did it.

uncertainty.title: Uncertainty and statistical ties
uncertainty.body: Epoch publishes a standard error on every row and LMArena publishes a confidence interval on every rating. That data was in the sources from day one and was dropped on the way to the page. It is now propagated to the composite and shown.
uncertainty.why: It is needed because the table is far tighter than its own precision. Right now the median gap between neighbouring models is {medianGap} composite points, while Epoch's median per-benchmark standard error runs from {stderrLow} to {stderrHigh} points. Publishing a strict order over differences that small promises a precision the measurement does not have: today {identicalPairs, plural, =0 {no pair sits less than a hundredth apart, but that is this run, not a rule} one {one pair sits less than a hundredth apart} other {# pairs sit less than a hundredth apart}}.
uncertainty.formula: Everything is carried as the half-width of a 95% interval. Epoch's standard error is multiplied by 1.96; LMArena's interval is already at 95% and is only rescaled along with the rating. A category mean propagates as √(Σ e²)/n and the composite as √(Σ (wᵢ/W)² eᵢ²).
uncertainty.floor: The published figure is a floor, not an estimate. Two reasons, both pointing the same way: LiveBench publishes no per-row error, so its inputs contribute zero — on this run {measuredInputs} of {totalInputs} inputs carry a published error — and the formula assumes the categories are independent when they are not entirely. The real interval can only be wider.
uncertainty.sound: That asymmetry is what keeps it usable. An interval that can only widen still supports "these two overlap" but never "these two differ". So ties are declared and differences are not: two models without a tie mark may well be tied anyway.
uncertainty.rank: The rank is a significance rank, not a position in a sorted list: a model sits at one plus the number of models measurably ahead of it. Strictly-better models are counted rather than neighbours grouped, because overlap is not transitive — A can overlap B and B overlap C while A and C are cleanly separated. On this run, {ranked} ranked models leave {distinctRanks} distinct ranks, and {overlappingPairs} of {adjacentPairs} adjacent pairs overlap.
uncertainty.unknown: {withoutInterval, plural, =0 {Right now every ranked model carries an interval.} one {Today one model carries no interval because none of its sources publish an error.} other {Today # models carry no interval because none of their sources publish an error.}} They are compared as point values, the one place this calculation zero-fills, which is why their model page says so outright. The alternative — refusing to separate them from anyone — was worse: it lifted a model well behind the leader into a tie for first, in exchange for knowing less about it.

cohort.title: Cohort coupling in LMArena
cohort.body: Arena ratings are Bradley-Terry, not percentages, so they are min-max normalised against the cohort present in each build. That has a consequence which is not obvious: when a model with an extreme rating joins, everyone else's normalised value moves even though their raw ratings did not change.
cohort.measured: Measured on 2026-08-03 against that day's cohort: a new model 60 points above the best of the time moved the normalised value by 16.03 points on average and 24.29 in the worst case — 2.40 and 3.64 composite points. Against today's median gap between neighbours ({medianGap} points), a shift like that is enough to reorder the table on its own.
cohort.disclosure: So every run records the raw delta and the normalised delta separately. When the normalised one moves and the raw one does not, the model page says so: cohort recalibration, not a change in measurement. A model can lose places without anyone voting differently, and that distinction belongs to the reader, not to us.
cohort.notchanged: The normaliser was not changed. Replacing min-max with a z-score was tried on 2026-08-03 and rejected with the measurement in hand: against that day's cohort it moved 16 of 44 models with 2.27 points of mean drift and could not show the new position was more correct than the old one, so it introduced movement without introducing truth. It also does not fix the problem — the mean and standard deviation depend on the cohort exactly as much as the min and max do — and the sigmoid proposed on top compresses precisely the head of the table, which is where readers look. Genuinely decoupling would need a fixed anchor across builds, and that is a separate study nobody has done yet.
cohort.threshold: The notice does not use a fixed threshold. It appears when the effect on the composite reaches the median gap between neighbouring models in that same run ({medianGap} points today), which is exactly the size at which a shift can change places. The threshold therefore retunes itself as the table tightens or spreads, instead of freezing one day's judgement. The other half of the notice — "the rating barely moved" — is {stillPoints} rating points, checked against the series itself: across {transitions} consecutive transitions in the history, the median movement is {moveMedian} and the 75th percentile is {moveP75}.

rejections.title: Guards that fired
rejections.body: The rejection policies are stated all over this page. This is where they show their work: a guard nobody can see fire is indistinguishable from one that never runs. Every run records the snapshots it rejected, with the observed ratio, the threshold, and which one was used instead.
rejections.none: No snapshot was rejected on the last run. That means the mislabelled-slice filter resolved everything that arrived, not that the guard is off: it is still measured on the raw rows, before deduplication, precisely so that it can fire.
rejections.cadence: Separate from rejection is ageing, which is a different failure: a source can fetch perfectly and still be serving numbers from months ago. Age is measured against each source's declared rhythm, and that rhythm is checked, on every run, against the one the source actually kept. LiveBench declares {declared} days; its observed median across {snapshots} published snapshots is {median}, so the declaration holds. Its longest gap was {longest} days, and during that gap the degraded state did fire, at {degraded}. LiveBench also adds models to its current snapshot without changing its date, so its age counts from the last model it published, and each of its numbers carries the date of the first daily ingest that saw it, never one earlier than its snapshot. local.title: What runs on my machine: memory fit
local.body: The Local page sizes open-weights models for a machine you describe. It is arithmetic on published sizes and nothing there feeds the composite, a rank or the coverage gate. The sizing data is a catalogue maintained by llmfit, joined to scored models by exact normalised name; where several repositories share a name, the most downloaded is used and the disagreement in size is published per row in data/local_models.json.
local.memory: Memory needed is weights plus KV cache plus 0.5 GB of runtime allowance. Weights are parameters × bytes per parameter by quantisation (Q8_0 1.05, Q6_K 0.80, Q5_K_M 0.68, Q4_K_M 0.58, Q3_K_M 0.48, Q2_K 0.37). The KV cache is 2 × full-attention layers × KV heads × head size × context × 2 bytes. The default context is 8,192 tokens or the model's own maximum if smaller. The best quantisation that fits within 98% of the pool is chosen; if none does, the context is halved once and the search is repeated.
local.bands: The verdict is memory use against the pool the model runs in: up to 60% roomy, up to 85% comfortable, up to 98% tight, above that it does not fit. Only a model fully resident on the GPU can be roomy; models that spill into RAM or run on the CPU are capped at comfortable. A pool filled past 98% does not load in practice.
local.modes: Run modes: GPU (everything in video memory); mixture-of-experts with the active experts in video memory and the rest in RAM; GPU plus RAM, where layers that do not fit are kept in RAM; CPU only. On unified memory there is one pool and nothing to spill into.
local.speed: Speed is memory bandwidth ÷ gigabytes read per token × 0.55, where 0.55 stands for kernel overhead, KV-cache reads and memory-controller loss. Mixture-of-experts models read active parameters only. Spilled layers and offloaded experts are read from system RAM at 50 GB/s, then scaled by the run mode. With no GPU bandwidth entered, no GPU speed is shown rather than a guessed one.
local.limits: What this does not do: hybrid attention layouts are used only where the data records one (config/local.json), so other models are sized as full attention and their memory is over-stated; mixture-of-experts speed on a GPU that holds every expert is an upper bound; pre-quantised formats, multi-GPU clusters and prompt-processing time are not modelled. In a comparison with llmfit's own output on about 6,800 catalogue entries, the fit verdict agreed in 98% of cases at 8 GB of video memory and 97% at 12 GB, and the run mode in 99%; the quantisation and memory figure agreed in about 91% to 93%, mostly because of catalogue versions and llmfit's name-based parameter corrections.
local.attribution: Attribution: the sizing arithmetic is ported from llmfit (https://github.com/AlexsJones/llmfit), MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 Alex Jones. The catalogue it reads is llmfit's hf_models.json under the same licence.

aliases.title: Name-matching audit
aliases.intro: Every source calls the same model something different: "claude-opus-5_max" on Epoch, "claude-opus-5-max-effort" on LiveBench, "claude-opus-5-max" on LMArena. The ingest collapses them onto one canonical key. If that collapse is wrong, one model is credited with another's numbers — the worst failure this project can have, and the only one it cannot detect on its own. So the whole mapping is published.
aliases.counts: {models} models, {names} published names matched onto them. In {ambiguous} cases a single source contributed more than one name to the same key: that is where a bad collapse would hide, so those are the ones worth checking first.
aliases.report: If you spot a bad match, you do not need to be a contributor to say so:
aliases.reportLink: open an issue with the form pre-filled
aliases.scoredNote: Every name that matched the canonical key is listed, not only the ones that score. Only the names belonging to the model's chosen configuration — shown under its name — feed the composite. In the LMArena column, the highlighted name is the row that actually scores.
aliases.integrityBody: Every run hashes what it downloaded. The "upstream" digest covers the bytes the publisher served: download the same URL, take its SHA-256, and it has to match. The "normalised" digest covers what the ingest made of those bytes, which is what /data is built from. If upstream matches and normalised does not, the change is ours.
aliases.paginated: Paginated source: {requests} requests this run, so the normalised payload digest is published instead of a URL list nobody could check by hand.
aliases.scoredMarker: this is the row that scores
